units.name: cli-arg-parsing
units.description: This is the part of ripgrep that understands the command a user typed. It defines every flag ripgrep accepts (like -i for case-insensitive, --json for machine-readable output, --type for file-type filtering), reads any saved configuration file and relevant environment variables, and combines all of that into one validated bundle of settings (HiArgs). It also produces ripgrep's --help text, its man page, and the tab-completion scripts for bash/fish/zsh/powershell, all generated from the same flag definitions so they never go out of sync. Everything else in ripgrep is handed this finished bundle of settings and never has to think about raw command-line text again. This unit must never actually perform a search, print a match, or walk a directory itself; its job stops at producing a validated, ready-to-use configuration (or, for --help/--version/completions, ready-to-print text) and handing off control.
units.role: Parses argv + config file + env vars into ripgrep's validated HiArgs configuration, and generates help/man/completions text.

units.name: search-orchestration
units.description: This is the control center of the rg command-line tool. When someone runs rg with a search pattern, this code figures out what needs to be searched (a list of files, a whole directory tree, or piped-in text), picks the right search engine and result formatter, and then drives the actual searching, either one file at a time or across many files at once using multiple threads. It also decides what to print when things go wrong, tracks whether an error happened (to set the program's exit code), prints optional timing/match statistics at the end, and offers a simple experimental 'search a prebuilt index instead of scanning files' mode. It is the glue that turns already-parsed command-line options into the actual work ripgrep does and the final text a user sees. It must never itself decide how a pattern matches or how files are formatted for output -- those decisions belong to the engines and printers it drives.
units.role: Top-level engine that wires together the walker, matcher, searcher, and printer to execute rg's search/list/generate modes and reports the process exit status.

units.name: glob-matching
units.description: This unit is a self-contained library for understanding and using glob patterns, the familiar wildcard notation people use to describe groups of files, like *.rs, **/target/, or src/**/*.{js,ts}. It takes a pattern written as text, checks that it is well-formed, and turns it into a fast internal matcher that can be asked, for any given file path, whether that path matches. It also supports checking many patterns against one path at once, as ripgrep needs when deciding whether a file should be searched or skipped based on many gitignore-style rules. It must never silently mis-parse a pattern in a way that causes a file the user expects to be included to be skipped, or a file the user expects to be excluded to be searched, since the correctness of --glob/--iglob and of gitignore-based file skipping both depend entirely on this logic being exactly right.
units.role: Compiles and matches Unix/gitignore-style glob patterns; a pure, dependency-light pattern-matching library.

units.name: gitignore-walk
units.description: This unit decides which files and folders rg should actually look inside when you run a search. It walks the directory tree you pointed it at, and along the way it reads the same kind of ignore rules Git itself understands (.gitignore, .ignore, .rgignore, per-repo excludes, and your global git ignore file) plus any include/exclude overrides and file-type filters given on the command line, so that build artifacts and other files you don't care about are skipped automatically. It must never silently skip a file the user explicitly named or explicitly included (an explicit request always wins over an ignore rule), and it must never search something the user explicitly excluded. It can walk single- or multi-threaded for speed.
units.role: Recursively enumerates 'the files worth searching' by combining gitignore-style rules, overrides, and file-type filters.

units.name: regex-engine
units.description: This is the piece of ripgrep that turns a search pattern typed by a user into a compiled, fast text-matching engine, and then uses that engine to answer whether a chunk of text matches and exactly where. It wraps Rust's own regex engine, translating ripgrep-specific concepts (smart case, whole-line/word matching, treating a pattern as literal text, never matching across a line boundary) into the lower-level regex machinery, and tries to pull out fast literal substrings so searching huge files can skip most of the text. It must never claim a match where the text doesn't actually satisfy the pattern, and must never fail to report a real match. It is interchangeable with pcre2-engine behind the same matcher-trait interface, which is why it is classified as an infra adapter rather than domain logic.
units.role: Compiles ripgrep's pattern syntax and matching options into Rust's regex engine and exposes it via the shared Matcher interface.

units.name: pcre2-engine
units.description: This is an optional, swappable pattern-matching engine ripgrep can use instead of its default one. It is only enabled when the program is built with the 'pcre2' feature and the user passes the -P/--pcre2 flag. It uses the PCRE2 C library, which supports advanced pattern features (backreferences and lookaround) that ripgrep's default matcher cannot handle, at the cost of being generally slower and requiring the PCRE2 library at build/link time. It must never introduce filesystem, network, or other side effects beyond pattern compilation and matching; its whole job is to answer whether a piece of text matches a pattern, and where, in a way that's interchangeable with the default engine.
units.role: Optional PCRE2-backed implementation of the matcher-trait Matcher interface, selected via the -P/--pcre2 flag.

units.name: line-searcher
units.description: This is the engine that actually reads through a file, or any stream of bytes, and figures out which lines match what the user is searching for. It is handed a matcher that knows how to test a chunk of bytes against the user's pattern, and a caller-supplied receiver for results. Its job is to feed data through the matcher line by line (or, in multi-line mode, across several lines at once), keep track of line numbers, gather requested context lines before and after each match, detect and safely handle binary or improperly encoded data, and hand back each match to the caller. It must never report a match on the wrong line number, never crash or hang on binary or invalid-encoding input, and must correctly handle binary data according to the caller's chosen policy. This is the actual search algorithm at the heart of the tool, not generic plumbing, which is why it is domain logic rather than infra.
units.role: Reads bytes from a file/reader/slice, drives a Matcher over them line-by-line (or multi-line), and reports matches plus context to a caller-supplied Sink.

units.name: result-printer
units.description: This unit turns the raw information that ripgrep's search engine finds (which file, which line, which bytes matched) into the actual text the user sees or that other programs consume. It offers three styles of output: the familiar colored, human-readable listing with line numbers and context; a line-by-line JSON format for scripts and editor integrations; and a compact summary format that reports counts or matching file names (for -c and -l). It also knows how to turn a matched file path into a clickable hyperlink, and keeps aggregate statistics (elapsed time, matches, bytes searched) for the end-of-run summary. It must never corrupt the byte-for-byte content of a match, never emit malformed JSON, never miscount matched lines or files, and never leak color or hyperlink escape codes when the destination does not want them.

units.name: index-experimental
units.description: This is an experimental, off-by-default feature of ripgrep that tries to speed up repeated searches over the same folder by building a small on-disk index file ahead of time. The idea is that instead of re-scanning every file from scratch on every search, ripgrep could first check a pre-built index to quickly rule out files that can't possibly match. Right now this unit only handles finding or creating the index database file on disk (in a .ripgrep folder or a path given via RIPGREP_INDEX_PATH) and a separate, not-yet-connected piece of logic that can turn a search pattern into a query over short text fragments (trigrams); it does not yet actually store or look up per-file information, so ripgrep currently falls back to a full, exhaustive search even when index mode is turned on. Because this is unfinished, the project's own documentation flags it as having 'very serious bugs' and keeps it behind an opt-in build flag. Whenever the missing piece is completed, it must never trust the index for a file that has changed since the index was built; there is currently no such staleness check at all.
units.role: Experimental on-disk index format meant to accelerate repeated searches by pre-computing trigram/literal facts about files; currently only implements index-file discovery/create/open.

units.name: matcher-trait
units.description: This unit defines the plug-socket that lets ripgrep swap in different pattern-matching engines (the built-in Rust regex engine, or the optional PCRE2 engine) without the rest of the program needing to know which one is in use. It doesn't itself search anything; it specifies the shape that any 'thing that can find a pattern in text' must have, plus a couple of small helper pieces, like safely substituting capture-group references into a replacement string for the -r/--replace flag. It must never itself decide how matching works or perform any actual searching, and its capture-group substitution logic must never read or write text outside the bounds of an actual match.
units.role: Defines the Matcher/Captures trait contract (plus supporting types) that decouples ripgrep's search/print/core logic from any specific regex/PCRE2 engine implementation.

units.name: cli-support
units.description: This is the toolbox of small, careful routines ripgrep uses to talk safely to the operating system and the terminal, rather than to search files. It answers questions like: is there real data waiting on stdin? Should output be flushed line-by-line or in big chunks? How do I show a file name that contains unusual bytes without garbling the screen? How do I run an external program like gzip or xz to decompress a file and get a good error message if that fails? What is this machine's hostname? It must never hang waiting for input that will never come, never corrupt the display when file names or search text contain unusual bytes, and never leave a spawned helper program running in the background after ripgrep is done with it.

violations_observed.location: crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs (HiArgs::haystack_builder, search_worker, etc.) and crates/core/flags/parse.rs (calls to logger::init, messages::set_messages/set_ignore_messages)
violations_observed.note: cli-arg-parsing and search-orchestration depend on each other's entrypoints (a genuine dependency cycle between two domain units): hiargs.rs constructs search-orchestration's HaystackBuilder/SearchWorkerBuilder/Printer/PatternMatcher types, while search-orchestration's main.rs calls cli-arg-parsing's parse() to obtain HiArgs and parse.rs calls search-orchestration's Logger::init/set_messages directly. This is an architectural finding rather than an unlisted-entrypoint violation -- both sides only touch items each unit already lists as an entrypoint -- but the tight bidirectional coupling means these two units cannot be versioned or reasoned about fully independently.
